weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution directly adapts Kang et al. (2025)'s self-certainty metrics from LLMs to VLAs using condition-masking as reference. The condition-masking reference construction is intuitive but represents only incremental adaptation without conceptual breakthrough.

Weak theoretical justification: Claims that masking creates an 'uncertainty-aware reference' lack rigorous support. No principled justification for KL divergence direction (Q||P), and choice of regularization temperature τ=4.0 and token aggregation strategy (first 5 tokens) are empirically driven rather than theoretically grounded.

Significant dataset-specific engineering requirements: Method requires per-dataset tuning of masking variants (text, state, or both), hyperparameters (τ, N, regularization temperature), and aggregation strategies. Different masking variants optimal for different environments, raising serious generalization concerns.

Joint training strategy lacks clarity: Presented as simple data augmentation with random condition dropout rather than a novel training paradigm. Insufficient explanation of why this improves condition-masking distributions beyond vague regularization claims. Dropout percentages (10%/10%/10%) appear arbitrary with no ablation.

Missing critical baselines and comparisons: No direct empirical comparison to concurrent verifier-based methods (Nakamoto et al. 2024, Kwok et al. 2025), which are the most relevant alternatives. Uniform KL baseline marginally outperformed in only one ablation.

Confounded real-world evaluation: Baseline comparisons use joint training + MG-Select versus baseline without joint training, making improvements attributable to either component. Only 4 ID tasks and 2 OOD tasks with 24/16 trials respectively—small scale for robotics claims.

Fragile aggregation heuristics: Table 5(f) reveals counterintuitive results where summation fails, averaging performs poorly, and only 'first 5 tokens' succeeds. Post-hoc justification by tokenizer structure suggests method is tightly coupled to specific model architectures rather than principled design.
Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance tests despite small real-world sample sizes. Real-world improvements (28-35%) may be within noise given evaluation scale.

Limited analysis and insights: No failure case analysis, no investigation into when/why masking-based confidence works or fails, and observations about task properties (e.g., model memorization) are mentioned but not explored systematically.
